title: 51 Indian Nationals Killed Fighting for Russia as Death Toll Nearly Doubles in a Year
excerpt: Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri confirms 227 Indians recruited into Russian armed forces, 139 discharged; families still await remains and compensation.
body:
• India confirms 51 Indian nationals have died after being recruited into the Russian armed forces — nearly double the 26 deaths reported to Parliament in December 2025.
  • Of the 227 Indians tracked by the government, 139 have been discharged through diplomatic intervention; roughly two dozen are believed to still be serving.
  • Most recruits were lured to Russia between 2022 and 2025 with promises of civilian jobs in construction and hospitality, only to have their passports confiscated and be pushed into military contracts.
  • The Supreme Court has directed the MEA to appoint a nodal officer, arrange DNA testing, and help families file compensation claims with the Russian Embassy.

A Death Toll That Keeps Climbing

Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri disclosed the latest figures on Monday during a briefing on Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Kyrgyzstan. "At last count, we had information about 227 Indian nationals who had been recruited into the Russian army," Misri said. "Out of that, we have information that 139 of our nationals have been discharged from the army. And unfortunately, of course, we have information also about 51 people who have perished so far."

https://x.com/ferozwala/status/2094145330766020683

The numbers trace a grim escalation. In December 2025, the Ministry of External Affairs told the Rajya Sabha that 202 Indians had been recruited and 26 had died. By May 2026, a Supreme Court status report put the tally at 217 recruits and 49 deaths, with six confirmed missing and 23 others unaccounted for. In late July, the government told the court that 51 were dead or missing and that 29 sets of mortal remains had been repatriated.

"This is an issue that we are in constant discussions with the Russian side."

— Vikram Misri, Foreign Secretary of India

Recruited Under False Pretenses

According to court filings and government disclosures, most of the men travelled to Russia between 2022 and 2025 on student, tourist, or work-related visas. They were promised civilian jobs — driving, construction, hospitality, cooking — by recruitment agents operating largely in northern and central Indian states including Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Uttarakhand, and Himachal Pradesh.

On arrival, families say, agents confiscated passports and pushed the men into short military contracts. Some were offered signing bonuses of roughly $5,000, monthly salaries of about $2,500, and death compensation of approximately $168,000, according to submissions the government made to the Supreme Court. Others say they had no choice: serve or face imprisonment.

The story of Ravi Moun, a 22-year-old from Haryana killed in action after being sent to Russia for what he was told would be a transportation job, became a flashpoint. "He was trained to dig trenches and later sent to the frontline," his brother Ajay Moun told reporters. "We remained in touch with him till March 12 and he was quite upset."

Diplomatic Effort Secures Most Discharges

India has secured the discharge of 139 nationals through sustained diplomatic engagement. Prime Minister Modi raised the issue directly with President Vladimir Putin during his 2024 visit to Moscow. Russia said it had stopped recruiting Indians, but new cases continued to surface through 2024 and 2025.

Misri said the Indian Embassy in Moscow "is monitoring this situation regularly with regard to the release and repatriation of these Indian citizens." About two dozen Indians are believed to still be in Russian military service.

Identification and Repatriation Remain Agonizingly Slow

Bringing the dead home has proved agonizing. Some remains lie in or near active combat zones. Russian casualty records are incomplete. The government has facilitated the repatriation of remains for an initial group and arranged local cremation for two others with family consent.

DNA samples from relatives of the dead and missing have been shared with Russian authorities to match bodies in morgues. The Supreme Court, hearing petitions from families across multiple states, directed the MEA to appoint a nodal officer in Delhi, arrange DNA testing, help families file compensation claims, and provide information in regional languages.

In at least one case, an Indian recruit is serving a prison sentence in Russia. Indian law prohibits citizens from fighting for a foreign army, and enforcement agencies have pursued the recruitment networks.

What's Next

The MEA has repeatedly warned citizens against overseas job offers from unregistered agents. But for the 51 families already told their sons or brothers are dead, and others among the 227 recorded cases still waiting for confirmation, the official numbers have not ended the wait for bodies, documents, or the compensation that contracts promised.

India's diplomatic leverage is constrained by its broader relationship with Moscow — one built on defense procurement, energy imports, and a historically close partnership that both sides describe as a "special and privileged strategic relationship." How aggressively New Delhi presses for accountability, beyond securing discharges, will be closely watched.
image_caption: India has confirmed that 51 nationals recruited into the Russian armed forces have died, nearly double the toll reported to Parliament in December 2024.
nri_angle: Indian nationals recruited abroad under false pretenses have been killed in a foreign war, raising urgent questions about protections for Indians seeking employment overseas.
author: Diaspora Desk
